article.headline: When the Agent Rewrites Its Own Playbook
article.lede: Most AI systems improve by updating their parameters — an expensive process requiring curated data and significant compute. A preprint from a seventeen-person research collective proposes a third way: keep the model weights frozen and let the agent rewrite its own library of reusable skills from live experience instead. The framework arrives just as open-source practitioners have independently converged on almost the identical design.
article.body:
Most discussions of making AI systems smarter reach for one of two tools: train the model on more data (*pre-training*, with costs measured in GPU-months and trillion-token corpora) or *fine-tune* it on curated examples — risking **catastrophic forgetting**, where acquiring new competencies erases old ones. A preprint from a research group calling itself the Memento-Team introduces a third column: **deployment-time learning**, formalized as M_{t+1} ← Write(M_t, r_t), where M is an external skill memory and r is the reward signal from a live interaction. The model weights stay frozen; only the memory grows.

The authors formalize this under a *Stateful Reflective Decision Process* (SRDP) — a variant of the standard reinforcement-learning framework augmented with episodic memory so that each task leaves a trace the next can draw on. Skills are stored as multi-artifact folders containing code, prompts, and declarative specifications in markdown, rather than flat functions. A skill *router*, trained via *offline reinforcement learning* to predict execution success (not semantic similarity), selects the appropriate skill for each task. When a skill fails, the system performs *credit attribution* — isolating which skill is responsible — rewrites it in-place, runs it against a unit-test gate, and rolls back if the rewrite degrades performance. Three rounds of self-improvement lifted GAIA performance by 26 percent and *HLE* performance by 116 percent in relative terms over the system's own pre-improvement baseline.

When the preprint surfaced, Teknium — co-founder of Nous Research and architect of the open-source *Hermes Agent* — wrote that it read like “someone saw hermes agent and wrote a paper on our memory/skill system.” Hermes had independently arrived at a structurally similar architecture: skills are markdown files stored under the agentskills.io open standard; a background reflection agent spawns after each completed task, deciding what is worth remembering and encoding new skills without interrupting foreground work. Nous Research has since shipped *Hermes Curator*, which consolidates and prunes the self-generated skill library automatically. That two groups working in apparent isolation — one academic, one practitioner — converged on near-identical designs is itself a signal: the same constraints (frozen weights, cheap adaptation, reusable procedural memory) keep producing the same answer.

The research lineage is well-established. *Voyager* (2023) built an ever-growing JavaScript skill library for Minecraft-playing agents, retrieved by semantic similarity. *ExpeL* extracted generalizable natural-language heuristics from past trajectories. *LATM* (Large Language Models as Tool Makers) tasked one model with writing Python utilities for a second to consume. Memento-Skills' formal contribution is the SRDP framework and a convergence proof under bounded rewards. Its practical distinguishing feature is the mutation-with-rollback loop: unlike Voyager's append-only library, Memento-Skills rewrites and replaces underperforming skills rather than simply accumulating them.

The larger implication is a shift in where learning lives. If deployment-time learning matures, the marginal cost of an agent becoming competent at a new task could approach near-zero — no fine-tune job queued, no dataset curated, no GPU spun up. That is attractive for enterprise deployments and for open-source projects like Hermes that run on modest hardware. Questions the paper does not fully resolve: what happens to skill libraries that compound errors over thousands of interactions; how do you audit a skill rewritten by an agent that was itself wrong; and whether the theoretical convergence guarantee holds when the LLM generating rewrites is unreliable. These are variants of questions the robotics field has asked about *online learning* for a decade, and they rarely have tidy answers.

concepts.definition: The foundational phase of building a large language model, in which the model's weights are optimized on massive corpora — typically hundreds of billions to trillions of tokens. The process requires significant GPU compute (often weeks on thousands of accelerators) and produces general language capabilities before any task-specific adaptation.

A second training phase that adapts a pre-trained model to specific tasks or behaviors using a much smaller dataset — typically thousands to hundreds of thousands of examples. Methods include supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and direct preference optimization (DPO). Fine-tuning updates the model's weights and requires meaningful compute, though far less than pre-training.

A well-documented failure mode in neural networks where learning a new task causes the model to lose competence on previously learned tasks. Both old and new knowledge are encoded in the same set of weights, so gradient updates for new tasks overwrite old ones. It is a primary practical concern when fine-tuning models on narrow task data.

A paradigm in which an AI system's model weights are never updated after initial training, but the system still improves over time by accumulating experience in an external memory or skill library. Adaptation occurs purely through what is written into and retrieved from that memory, with no gradient computation required. The Memento-Skills paper formalizes this as M_{t+1} ← Write(M_t, r_t).

A formal framework introduced in the Memento-Skills paper that extends the standard Markov decision process by augmenting the agent's state with episodic memory M. Because memory grows with each interaction, the raw trajectory is non-Markovian; SRDP recovers the Markov property by treating the augmented state (task state plus skill memory) as the unit of analysis. The paper proves convergence of soft policy iteration in this framework under bounded rewards.

A variant of reinforcement learning in which an agent is trained on a fixed dataset of previously collected experiences, rather than by interacting live with an environment. This avoids the safety and cost risks of live exploration but requires the historical data to cover the scenarios the agent needs to learn from. Memento-Skills uses it to train the skill router on historical execution-success signals.

In Memento-Skills and similar agent frameworks, the component responsible for selecting which skill from the library to apply to a given task. Unlike simpler approaches that retrieve by cosine similarity between embeddings, Memento-Skills trains its router via offline reinforcement learning to predict which skill will actually succeed on execution — a behavior-aligned objective rather than a text-similarity one.

The process of determining which specific component of a system caused a failure in a multi-step pipeline. In Memento-Skills, when an agent fails at a task, credit attribution isolates which skill file is responsible, enabling targeted rewriting of that skill rather than indiscriminate modification of the whole library.

A benchmark for evaluating general AI assistants on tasks requiring multi-step reasoning, web research, and tool use — tasks that are difficult for current language models but relatively straightforward for humans. Tasks are graded on exact-match answers and span domains including coding, browsing, and multi-modal reasoning. Published by researchers at Meta and Hugging Face.

A benchmark consisting of extremely difficult graduate-level questions across academic disciplines, designed to probe the frontier of current AI capabilities. The questions were crowdsourced from researchers specifically to be beyond the reach of existing models. A high score on HLE indicates strong generalization to novel, expert-level reasoning.

A 2023 research system from Caltech and NVIDIA that demonstrated open-ended, lifelong learning in Minecraft by maintaining an ever-growing library of executable JavaScript skills, each stored with a natural-language description and retrieved by semantic similarity. Voyager is append-only — it does not rewrite or delete existing skills — and served as an influential proof-of-concept for the skill-library paradigm.

An agent framework that extracts generalizable natural-language heuristics from a pool of past task trajectories, using them to guide behavior on new tasks without updating model weights. ExpeL produces text-based insights rather than executable code, making them flexible but less precise than skill libraries.

concepts.term: LATM (Large Language Models as Tool Makers)
concepts.definition: A framework in which a more capable LLM writes Python utility functions (tools) that a smaller, cheaper LLM then uses. Tools are cached and reused across tasks, reducing the need for the larger model in routine operations. The system does not support skill mutation and tools must be pure Python — no external APIs.

In machine learning and robotics, online learning refers to a system's ability to update its model or policy continuously from live experience, in contrast to training once on a fixed dataset. The field has long grappled with challenges of stability (avoiding catastrophic forgetting), safety (exploration that does not damage hardware), and drift (what happens when errors compound over time).

repos.summary: The official implementation of the Memento-Skills self-evolving agent framework, accompanying the arXiv preprint of the same name. The system stores reusable skills as multi-artifact markdown folders, uses an offline-RL-trained router to select them, and mutates underperforming skills in-place via a reflection loop with rollback. Supports open-source LLMs including Kimi, MiniMax, and GLM, with both CLI and GUI interfaces.

Nous Research's open-source autonomous agent, built by Teknium and team. Hermes independently implements a structurally similar skill-library architecture: skills are markdown files following the agentskills.io open standard, and a background reflection agent synthesizes new skills from completed tasks without interrupting foreground work. Ships with 131 built-in skills, 68 tools, and integrations with 15-plus messaging platforms.

article.fact_check: The Memento-Skills paper (arXiv:2603.18743, March 2026) is an arXiv preprint and has not yet undergone peer review. The benchmark improvements — 26 percent on GAIA and 116 percent on HLE — are relative figures over the system's own ablation baselines, not head-to-head comparisons against external state-of-the-art systems, which limits their interpretive weight. The convergence guarantee cited from the companion Memento 2 paper relies on bounded rewards, an assumption that may not hold in all open-ended deployment scenarios.

poster_teknium.blurb: Teknium is an AI researcher and developer known for contributions to open-source language models, particularly in the alignment and fine-tuning space. They post about machine learning, model training techniques, and AI safety. Their follower count is not publicly available due to restricted access.
